clue.text: Our present circumstances may be novel

blocks.note: first meaning: the manner of our life these days
second meaning: the title of Anthony Trollope's satirical novel of 1875

explanation.surface: Someone muses that our current situation might be something new and unprecedented.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like an adjective meaning new; it is the noun, a work of fiction by Trollope.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes current living conditions literally, and it is also the title of a famous Victorian book by Trollope.

clue.text: Sort of reproduction in earphones gets distorted

indicators.note: something distorted is twisted out of its proper shape, so the letters before it are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written: fifteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A sound reproduction played through earphones comes out distorted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reproduction' suggests audio playback, which suits earphones; here it is biological, the breeding of offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: Parthenogenesis is a kind of reproduction in which an egg develops without fertilisation, as in aphids.

clue.text: Man using force, one out to be evil

indicators.note: out means removed, so the letter for one is dropped from the word meaning using force

blocks.note: a man is a male
violent means using physical force
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A thug who uses force is someone set on doing evil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One out' looks like a person leaving, but it tells you to drop the numeral one from the word for using force.
explanation.definitionFit: Malevolent means wishing harm on others, so it serves as a synonym for wicked or evil.

clue.text: Vessel set out towards a foreign sea

indicators.note: set out can mean laid out differently, so the three letters of set are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written
mer is French for sea

explanation.surface: A ship has departed, heading for the waters of some other country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set out' reads as the ship departing, but 'out' only tells you to rearrange 'set'.
explanation.definitionFit: A steamer is a ship powered by steam engines, and a ship is a vessel.

clue.text: Regard daughter as offspring

blocks.note: to regard is to look at or see
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A parent is told to look on a daughter as their child.
explanation.definitionFit: Seed is a literary or biblical word for descendants, as in the seed of Abraham, so it means children.

clue.text: You can't write much on it - produce script at random

definitions.text: You can't write much on it

indicators.note: random means in no set order, so the letters before it are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written: fifteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A complaint that a small card leaves little room, so any writing on it is a random scribble.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash separates the definition from the wordplay; 'at' belongs to the fodder, not the indicator, which is just 'random'.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture postcard has a photograph on one side and only a small space for a message on the other.

clue.text: Northern town's funnier characters involved in arguments in pubs

indicators.note: characters are letters, and involved means tangled up, so the letters of the word before are shuffled
in places one group of letters inside another, here twice over

blocks.note: pubs are bars
rows are quarrels or arguments
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Comedians in a northern town tell jokes amid the rows in its pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two insertions: the jumbled letters go inside the arguments, and that goes inside the pubs. The town is a shipbuilding port in Cumbria, north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Barrow-in-Furness is a port and industrial town in Cumbria, in the north of England.

clue.text: Such finally gets bagged by countryman?

definitions.text: Such finally gets bagged by countryman?

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word just before it
something bagged is put in a bag, so this letter goes inside the word that follows

blocks.note: a peasant is a rural labourer, a countryman
the last letter of such

explanation.surface: A game bird ends up in the bag of a rural shooter.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: a pheasant is just what a countryman out shooting bags. H goes into PEASANT.
explanation.definitionFit: Pheasants are game birds commonly shot by country people, so the bird is what ends up in their game bag.

clue.text: I may enter strange place of large proportions

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so the single letter goes into the rearranged word
strange means odd or unusual, so the word after it appears in an unusual order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wonders if they might walk into an odd, enormous building.
explanation.definitionFit: Epical is a variant of epic, describing something on a heroic or grand scale, hence very large.

clue.text: Bandage the man following hit

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the man is placed second, after the word for hit

blocks.note: to swat is to hit sharply
the man is he

explanation.surface: A man gets his wound dressed after being struck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' tells you the man comes after the hit.
explanation.definitionFit: To swathe is to wrap something in layers of cloth, which is what bandaging a limb involves.

clue.text: It's experienced through hearing a unilateral declaration by politician

blocks.note: taken as written
UDI stands for Unilateral Declaration of Independence, as made by Rhodesia in 1965
a Tory is a British Conservative politician

explanation.surface: A politician's one-sided announcement is something people only know about from what they have heard.
explanation.walkthrough: UDI is the familiar abbreviation from Rhodesia's 1965 break from Britain; Tory is the everyday name for a member of the UK Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Auditory means relating to the sense of hearing, so an auditory sensation is one perceived by the ear.

clue.text: A neat dwelling

blocks.note: surface reading: a tidy little house
setter's reading: neat is an old word for cattle, so this is a home for cows

explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' looks like tidy, but it is the old word for oxen or cattle, still seen in neatsfoot oil.
explanation.definitionFit: A byre is a cowshed, the building where cattle are housed, especially in Scotland and northern England.

clue.text: Where we hear the canopy of power may be brought down

indicators.note: we hear means the words are judged by how they sound when spoken

blocks.note: the position the clue asks about: above
a canopy of state hangs over a throne, the seat of power

explanation.surface: A royal canopy is described as liable to be toppled.
explanation.walkthrough: Ask where a canopy of state sits: over the throne. Said out loud, that is OVERTHROWN.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruler who is overthrown has been toppled from power, which is to be brought down.

clue.text: Cloth goes with bathroom items

blocks.note: toile is a linen or cotton fabric
has goes, that is attempts or tries

explanation.surface: A towel is put out alongside the things kept in the bathroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes' is the noun plural, as in having goes at something.
explanation.definitionFit: Toiletries are soaps, shampoos and similar washing products kept in a bathroom.

clue.text: Dear little rodent coming back into place of rest

indicators.note: coming back means returning, so the rodent's name is read from its end
into means placed inside, so the turned word goes within the place of rest

blocks.note: a bed is where one rests
a vole is a small rodent

explanation.surface: A pet mouse returns to curl up in its sleeping spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Beloved means dearly loved, and dear is used as an adjective or noun of affection in the same way.

clue.text: Things making a bang give little boy endless fear

indicators.note: endless means without its end, so the last letter of the word for fear is dropped

blocks.note: Tim is a short form of a boy's name, Timothy
panic is sudden fear

explanation.surface: Fireworks going off leave a small lad terrified.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Things making a bang' suggests fireworks; here they are drums.
explanation.definitionFit: Timpani are kettledrums in an orchestra, instruments struck to produce a booming sound.

clue.text: In brotherhood ought you to appear valiant?

indicators.note: In says the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of brotherhood through ought to the start of you

explanation.surface: A question of whether members of a fraternity should seem courageous.
explanation.definitionFit: Doughty is an old-fashioned word for brave and determined, so it is a synonym of valiant.

clue.text: Maiden has one home recipe - one for possible first course

blocks.note: M is the cricket scorebook abbreviation for a maiden over
the Roman numeral for one
a nest is a home
R is short for recipe, from Latin, as on a prescription
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young woman owns a home recipe that might make a starter for dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: A maiden in cricket is an over with no runs scored. 'One' appears twice: first as I, then as itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Minestrone is an Italian vegetable soup, and soup is a typical starter served at the beginning of a meal.

clue.text: Muck that gets stomachs turning over

indicators.note: turning over flips something, so the informal word for stomachs is read backwards

blocks.note: tums is an informal word for stomachs

explanation.surface: Filth so disgusting it makes people feel queasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stomachs turning over' reads as nausea; it is the instruction to reverse a word for stomachs.
explanation.definitionFit: Smut means soot or a speck of dirt, as well as indecent material, so it is a kind of muck.

clue.text: Cutting grass outside always

indicators.note: outside means surrounding, so the word for grass goes round the word for always

blocks.note: in British slang to grass is to inform on someone, and so is to sing
ever means always, as in for ever

explanation.surface: Someone is forever out mowing the lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting grass' reads as mowing, but grass is the verb meaning to inform, as a criminal informer does.
explanation.definitionFit: Severing means cutting through or cutting off, so it works as a synonym for cutting.

clue.text: Wild animal in the same place no longer

blocks.note: ib. is the short form of ibidem, Latin for in the same place, used in footnotes
ex means former, so no longer what it was

explanation.surface: A creature that once lived here is no longer found there.
explanation.walkthrough: IB, like ibid, abbreviates ibidem, used in references to cite the same source again.
explanation.definitionFit: An ibex is a wild mountain goat of the Alps and other ranges, with long curved horns.

clue.text: New hesitation about monetary unit

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so the word for hesitation is written backwards

blocks.note: er is the sound of hesitating in speech
a cent is a unit of currency

explanation.surface: Fresh doubts are raised over a currency.
explanation.definitionFit: Recent means having happened or appeared lately, so it means new or fresh.

clue.text: Travelling doctor encounters bad temper

blocks.note: MO is a Medical Officer, a military doctor
bile is anger or irritability

explanation.surface: A doctor doing house calls meets an irritable patient.
explanation.definitionFit: Mobile means able to move about, like a travelling library or a mobile clinic.

clue.text: Speculator may get the gold first

blocks.note: taken as written
or is the heraldic word for gold
1st with the digit read as the letter I

explanation.surface: An investor hopes to be the first to get the gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speculator' suggests a financial gambler, which suits gold; here it means someone who speculates in ideas.
explanation.definitionFit: A theorist forms ideas and hypotheses about how things work, which is to speculate intellectually.
